prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I’m jotting down these lines, having borrowed a pen from a waitress in this roadside restaurant. Three rusty pines prop up the sky in the windows. My soup gets cold, which implies I’ll eat it cold. Soon I too will leave a tip on the table, merge into the beehive of travelers and board one of the ferries, where there’s always a line to the loo and no one knows where the captain is. Slightly seasick, I keep on writing of the wind-rose and lobster traps, seagulls, if any—and there always are. Check the air and you’ll see them above straw hats and caps. The sun at noon glides like a monstrous star- fish through clouds. Others drink iced tea, training binoculars on a tugboat. When I finish this letter, I’ll take a gulp from the flask you gave me for the road in days when I was too young to care about those on the pier who waved goodbye. I miss them now: cousins in linen dresses, my mother, you, boys in light summer shirts. Life is too long. The compass needle dances. Everything passes by. The ferry passes by ragged yellow shores.

I write these lines with a pen borrowed from a waitress at this roadside restaurant. Through the window, three weathered pines seem to hold up the sky. My soup grows cold—which is to say, I shall eat it cold. outputs.L3:
I am writing this letter with a pen I borrowed from the waitress, its ink running thin in places, at a roadside restaurant that smells of old coffee and diesel fumes. The soup in front of me has gone cold—a gray film has settled over its surface like the first skin of ice on a autumn pond—but I hadn't the heart to send it back. Outside the window, a row of pines stand rusted at their tips, needles browning from some blight or simply the slow work of the season, and I find myself oddly comforted by their imperfection. There is nothing remarkable about this place. That, perhaps, is what makes it worth writing down.

Soon I will fold this letter, however unfinished, and step out to join the crowd already gathering near the dock—travelers with their suitcases and their impatience, shuffling toward the ferry that will carry us across the water. I know already what awaits: the long line for the bathroom, the jostling for a seat by the railing, the particular tiredness that comes from waiting alongside strangers who are all, in their own way, going somewhere else. It is not glamorous, this kind of travel. But there is something honest in its inconvenience.

For now, though, I sit and watch the harbor through the smudged glass. Seagulls wheel overhead with their thin, complaining cries, circling the stacked lobster traps piled at the pier's edge like some strange geometry of rope and wire. A tugboat pushes slowly across the water, leaving behind it a wake that spreads and dissolves. The whole scene rocks gently—or perhaps it is only me, my stomach already anticipating the ferry's roll, that faint seasickness that comes not from the water yet but from the thought of it. The sea has a way of announcing itself before you've even left the shore.

I think, too, of the people I have left behind on other days like this one—the ones who stood at doorways and waved as I pulled away, and how many times I turned my back too soon, too eager for wherever I thought I was going. I did not understand then what it meant to be watched until you disappeared. Now I find myself missing them in a way I never allowed myself to before: the particular angle of my mother's hand lifted in farewell, the way my brother always looked a little sad even when he was smiling. I wish I had looked longer. I wish I had waved back with more feeling.

There is a strange arithmetic to time that I have never been able to solve. Each day, sitting in places like this, waiting for buses or ferries or the check to arrive, feels endless—an eternity contained in a bowl of cold soup and a borrowed pen. And yet, when I look back, the years seem to have gone by in an instant, as quickly as this ferry will cross the water and reach the other side. Everything passes, even when it feels as though it never will. Perhaps that is the only truth this letter can offer: that time is long only while we are living inside it, and short the moment we turn to look back.
outputs.L4:
**A Letter from the Water**

The soup has gone cold in its bowl—I noticed this only after the third spoonful, after the taste had already turned from warmth to something flatter, more honest. There is a strange clarity in cold soup, the way it refuses to pretend anymore. I am writing to you from a restaurant that exists only for people passing through, the kind of place with plastic chairs bolted to the floor and a menu that hasn't changed in a decade. Outside, seagulls argue over something in the gravel lot, their voices sharp and unbothered by my presence. The sun is doing what suns do at this hour—hanging low, indecisive, throwing long shadows across the tables where truckers and tourists sit without speaking to one another.

I keep thinking of the pier, of how you all stood there waving until you became small, then smaller, then just shapes I had to imagine rather than see. There's a particular cruelty in departures that happen slowly—the ship pulling away inch by inch, giving you time to watch love become distance. A quick goodbye would almost be kinder. But we don't get to choose the speed of these things.

Now I write from the ferry itself, some hours later, my stomach uncertain about the rhythm of the waves. Seasickness is a strange humility—it reminds you that you are, after all, just a body, subject to tides and motions larger than your will. I press my forehead against the cool window and watch the shoreline unspool like a ribbon, ragged and quick, here and then gone. Rocks, a lighthouse, someone's house with laundry on the line—all of it appearing and disappearing before I can hold onto any single image.

This is what travel does, I think: it compresses time into these strange, disjointed frames. One moment you are sitting across from someone you love, sharing a meal, complaining about the weather. The next, you are alone on a boat, nauseous, watching gulls trail the wake for scraps, and the person you love is just a memory of a wave on a pier that no longer exists except in your mind.

I don't know why, but somewhere between the cold soup and this rocking ferry, I arrived at a thought that felt truer than most of what I usually believe: life is too long. Not too short, as everyone always says, urging us to seize each day before it slips away—but too long, stretched out across all these separations we must endure, all these piers we must leave from, all these people we must watch grow small and then vanish into the shape of memory. We keep saying goodbye to people, to places, to versions of ourselves, and somehow we're expected to keep doing this, again and again, for years.

The shore continues to pass—ragged, brief, indifferent to my meditations. Somewhere behind me is the restaurant with its cold soup, the pier with its waving figures, and ahead is another shore I haven't yet learned the shape of. I suppose this is what it means to be in transit: existing in the gap between what you've lost sight of and what you haven't yet arrived at, seasick and searching, still writing letters to people who feel less like presences now and more like the coastlines you leave behind—beautiful, fragmented, and already becoming past tense.
outputs.L5:
# Three Steps Forward

There were three things she had promised herself before the year ended: to finish the manuscript, to call her estranged brother, and to finally learn how to swim properly instead of just paddling near the shore.

Soon, she told herself, tracing the word in the condensation on her coffee cup. Soon had become her favorite lie, the one she told without malice, the one that let her sleep at night while her ambitions gathered dust like unopened mail.

But something had shifted slightly in recent weeks—a subtle recalibration she couldn't quite name. Maybe it was the way autumn light fell differently through her window now, slightly more golden, slightly more insistent. Maybe it was turning thirty-four and feeling the quiet weight of accumulated soons pressing against her chest.

She opened her laptop. The manuscript file blinked at her, unchanged since March. Three chapters remained. She had written three sentences in the last three months. The math wasn't lost on her.

Her phone sat nearby, her brother's contact information three taps away. She'd rehearsed the conversation so many times it had worn smooth, like a stone handled too often. Three years of silence between them now, each month adding weight to the eventual reunion, making it feel simultaneously more necessary and more impossible.

Outside, she could see the community pool through bare branches, closing soon for the season. She'd bought the swim lessons package in June. Used it once.

Slightly overwhelmed, she made a decision that felt small but wasn't: she would do one thing today. Not three. Just one.

She picked up the phone.

The three rings before her brother answered stretched into something that felt like forever, and then, quite suddenly, didn't.

"Hey," she said, her voice slightly unsteady. "It's been too long."

Some sooner-thans, it turned out, arrived exactly when they were meant to—not a moment before, not a moment after. Just slightly, perceptibly, right on time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in the style of a letter written aboard a ferry, blending nostalgia with vivid maritime imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**Letter from the Crossing**

Dear one,

I write this with the railing's paint
flaking under my elbow, green going to rust,
and the whole gray afternoon
tilting slightly, the way memory does
when you press on it too hard.

We are somewhere between the last dock
and the one that hasn't arrived yet—
that particular nowhere I've always loved,
where the water doesn't belong to any town
and neither, for an hour, do I.

The gulls have followed us out
past the buoys, past the place
where the harbor smell gives way
to something cleaner, older, less forgiving.
They cry like they remember something too.

I keep thinking of that summer
we sat on a dock much smaller than this boat,
feet not touching water, just imagining the cold,
and you said the horizon was a kind of promise
the sea makes and never quite keeps.

I believe you more now.
The wake behind us unspools like a sentence
I can't finish, white foam already forgetting
its own shape, the way our old address
has probably forgotten the sound of our door.

There's a woman near the bow
holding a paper cup of coffee like a small fire.
A boy presses his whole face to the glass
to watch the water fold and fold again,
endlessly rewriting itself.

I want to tell you the light here
is doing something I don't have the word for—
not gold, not gray, but the color of almost,
of things about to become other things.

The engines hum beneath my feet
like a held note, patient, unbothered
by all this longing I've brought aboard,
this cargo of years I keep dragging
from shore to shore.

Somewhere ahead, land is gathering itself
into a shape I'll recognize.
Somewhere behind, the place we started
is already smaller than my thumb,
already turning into story.

I don't know why boats make me
write to you like this—
maybe because we are always
in the middle of crossing something,
and there's no pretending otherwise out here,

no solid ground to stand on
and lie about arriving.

Just the water,
doing what water does,
and me,
doing what I've always done—
missing you in the particular light
of unfinished distances.

More soon, when the shore comes clear.
For now: salt, engine-thrum, gray wing overhead—
and this small paper boat of words
I'm sending out to find you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a reflective, first-person poem about traveling by sea, incorporating details like seagulls, lobster traps, and a compass needle, with a wistful tone about lost time.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Long Crossing

I stood at the rail and watched the gulls
trail behind us like unfinished thoughts,
white commas punctuating the gray
sentence of the sky. They know
when to leave a thing alone,
when the wake grows cold and unremarkable—
unlike me, who keeps looking back
at where the shore used to be.

Somewhere below, lobster traps
sit stacked in coils of rope and rust,
waiting for the hands that set them
to haul up whatever the dark has kept.
I think of all I've lowered down
into years I can't get back—
small cages baited with intention,
pulled up empty, or not pulled up at all.

The compass needle trembles north
with a certainty I've never owned.
It doesn't ask what it's leaving,
doesn't grieve the water passed through,
only points, the way youth pointed once,
before I learned that direction
isn't the same as arrival,
that a heading can be true
and still cost you everything behind it.

I am somewhere between the harbor I left
and the one I'm told is coming.
The gulls have turned back now—
even they have limits to their following.
Only the needle stays constant,
indifferent to my wondering
whether the self who first set sail
is still aboard, or whether he stayed
on some dock I didn't notice passing,
waving at a ship that didn't see him,
that only knew to keep on going,
the way time does,
the way the sea forgives no one
for looking back too long
at what the water's already closed over.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that reads like an epistolary reflection from a roadside restaurant and a ferry journey, touching on memory, family, and the passage of life.
counterfactuals.output:
# Letter from the Crossing

I am writing this from a booth by the window,
where the coffee comes bottomless and the pie case
turns slowly, like something remembering itself.
Outside, gulls argue over the parking lot
the way you and I used to argue over maps,
neither of us willing to admit we were lost.

The waitress here has your mother's hands—
that same efficient tenderness, the way she sets
the check down like a small apology.
I ordered the meatloaf because you would have,
because some griefs are easier
to swallow than to name.

Later, on the ferry, the water went on
being water, indifferent and enormous,
the way time is indifferent, the way it carries
everything forward without asking permission.
I stood at the rail and thought of Dad
teaching us to skip stones, how he said

*it's all in the wrist, in letting go
at exactly the right moment*—
and I wonder now if he meant something else,
some larger physics of departure
he was trying to hand us
before his hands stopped working.

The gulls followed the boat for a while,
then didn't. That's the whole of it, maybe—
things follow you until they don't,
and you keep moving anyway,
because the far shore is real,
because someone is probably waiting there

with a car that needs gas,
with news that will keep or won't,
with a face that will look older
than the one you carry in your wallet,
folded soft at the corners
from all this handling.

I'll write again when I know
what I'm trying to say. For now:
the water is grey and then blue and then grey.
The horizon keeps its distance politely.
I miss you in the ordinary way—
which is to say, constantly, and without drama,

the way you miss a language
you used to dream in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical, image-rich poem in the tradition of Elizabeth Bishop, evoking coastal travel, nostalgia, and the sense of time slipping away.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Ferry at Low Tide

The pilings wear their green socks of moss
below the waterline, where the tide has left
its pencil marks, a hundred faded rulings
against the barnacled wood. I have counted them
before, on other mornings, with other coffee
cooling in a paper cup, the same gulls
wheeling like something thrown and not quite caught.

The ferry comes the color of an old nickel,
diesel-breathed, dependable as grief.
It has always just arrived, or just departed—
never the long clean moment of arrival
one might photograph. We board by feeling,
by the memory of feet on gangplanks,
the particular give of water underfoot
disguised as solid decking.

Somewhere behind us, the town rearranges
its clapboard houses into a smaller town,
then a color, then a thought we'll have again
at 3 a.m. in another state. The lighthouse
keeps its one eye on us like a mother
who has stopped waving but still stands
in the doorway, arms crossed, watching.

I have made this crossing enough times
to know the exact moment when the smell
of land gives way to the smell of going—
salt replacing woodsmoke, replacing
the specific rust of this particular dock,
these particular nails, weeping their orange
tears into the grain for forty years.

Time moves like the tide moves: not away,
exactly, but into a different relation
with the shore. What's left is what
the water couldn't carry: a bottlecap,
a single boot, the outline of a boat
long taken to some other use—
a chicken coop, perhaps, or firewood,
or nothing, just the ghost-shape
pressed into the sand like a fossil
of the afternoon we can't get back to,
though we keep circling in these waters,
looking for the place we must have entered,
thinking, *surely, it was here.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose-poem style piece narrated by someone writing a letter mid-journey, mixing sensory details of a seaside trip with longing for people left behind.
counterfactuals.output:
The train has stopped again, somewhere between one gray station and another, and I am writing to you with a pen that keeps skipping, the way my heart does when I think too long about the shape of your hands.

The sea, when it finally came into view past Marsh Junction, was not blue but pewter, the color of old spoons, the color of things that have been touched by too many hands and worn smooth. I pressed my palm to the window glass and felt how cold the world had become without you in it to warm the edges.

There is salt in the air here that reminds me of your skin after you swim, that particular brine of you, and I have been collecting small stones from a shore I have not yet reached, imagining the weight of them in your pocket, imagining you asking *where did this one come from* and me saying *from the place I went without you, the place that tasted like your absence*.

The gulls scream overhead in a language I almost understand—something about hunger, something about distance, something about the way the tide keeps leaving and coming back, leaving and coming back, the way I keep leaving and coming back to the thought of your face across the breakfast table, the crumbs, the light through the curtains, ordinary and unbearable in its ordinariness now that I am here and you are there.

I ate a peach on the platform at Aldermoor, juice running down my wrist like something urgent, like something I meant to tell you months ago and never did. The sweetness of it made me ache. Everything here makes me ache—the postcards I cannot choose between, the couples walking arm in arm along a boardwalk that goes nowhere I need to be, the lighthouse blinking its slow patient code across the water: *come back, come back, come back.*

I don't know when I'll arrive. The tracks curve away from the coast and then return to it, as if even the train cannot decide how close it wants to get to all this blue-gray longing. But when I do arrive—when I finally stand at the edge of that water with sand between my toes and your name still warm in my mouth—I will write you again, and this time I will tell you everything the sea would not let me say today: that I miss you like tide misses shore, constantly, physically, with the whole pull of the moon behind it.

Until then, I am folding this letter the way I fold my longing—small enough to carry, sharp enough at the corners to remind me it's there.

With salt-stained hands and a heart still homesick for yours,

*[unsigned, as if the ink itself might carry your name back to me]*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
